summary: We developed an earth jukebox that takes EIC visuals or any other visuals and converts it into sound, based off chosen parameters that best reflect the various elements of sound and music. It helps people with visual impairments to better appreciate visuals through sound, and people with different forms of disabilities through accessible controls to better appreciate them and get the message the visual is sending.
details:
How it works and what it does

Earth Sound Systems turns NASA Earth Information Center visuals and other earth-related visuals into music. A listener picks a “record”, which is a real frame from NASA’s Scientific Visualization Studio, such as night lights, ocean currents, smoke or forests. As a play head sweeps across the image, the jukebox performs it live in the browser.

The translation follows seven simple rules, and each one controls a single part of the music. Where something sits on the map sets its timing and pitch. Its colour chooses the instrument, its brightness sets the volume, and its size sets how long the note lasts. The amount of detail sets the tempo. The share of red, orange and magenta (heat, fire, smoke) sets the mood, with a heartbeat for the most urgent frames.

Benefits

Earth science is shared almost entirely through pictures, which leaves many people out. Globally, at least 2.2 billion people have a near or distance vision impairment. It opens NASA’s visuals to them, and gives sighted viewers a new way to feel what the data means: urgent frames really do sound urgent.

Intended Impact

We want Earth data to be something people can hear as well as see. We hope it helps blind and low-vision people explore science independently, and helps the public connect emotionally with how our planet is changing and appreciate it as a whole.

Tools and technologies

We built the site with HTML, CSS and JavaScript. The music is generated live with the Web Audio API, the 3D globe uses WebGL, and read-aloud uses the browser’s built-in speech. We used Python to prepare NASA’s images and to test the site. Our data comes from seven NASA Scientific Visualization Studio datasets, with NASA’s Caldwell 73 sonification as our starting point.

Creativity

Most sonifications are custom-made for one image. We designed a single rulebook that works on every Earth dataset, and even on uploaded photos, yet produces genuinely different music for each one.

Factors Considered

Our main challenge was keeping the music accurate to the data while making it pleasant to hear, so every note stays in key and the sound never becomes cluttered. We kept the rules few and distinct so they’re easy to learn. Accessibility guided the whole project: screen-reader support, read-aloud, captions, keyboard control, and a Safe mode for people sensitive to flashing or motion.
